title: How Leaders Can Build Judgment, Not Just Expertise
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership Field Note argues that organizations are very good at building expertise but far less deliberate about building judgment. Expertise explains how something works, while judgment decides what matters most when facts are incomplete, goals conflict and no rule quite fits. The note illustrates the gap with a power grid customer who demands a 20 percent credit after an outage: one manager cites the contract's 5 percent cap, while another weighs the relationship's three-year value, the precedent for other accounts and the values guiding the frontline. Leaders build judgment, the piece says, by exposing people to how decisions are made, asking what they would do and why, sharing their own trade-offs and debriefing afterward so the quality of thinking is separated from the luck of the outcome. The goal is a team that decides well when the leader is absent and the answer is not in the field manual.
points: Expertise answers known questions, whereas judgment weighs mixed goals and incomplete facts, and treating them as the same leaves teams of specialists who flounder off the playbook.
The credit-dispute example shows that a contract is one input to a decision, not the decision itself.
Leaders can grow judgment by explaining the trade-offs behind their decisions, including what they gave weight to and what they gave up.
Asking team members what they would do and why, then debriefing, builds a way of thinking one conversation at a time.
The measure of a leader's influence is how the team decides when the leader is not in the room.
quotes: Expertise tells you how something works. Judgment tells you what matters most when the facts are incomplete, the goals are mixed, and no rule quite fits the situation.
Leaders who confuse expertise and judgment end up with teams full of capable specialists who flounder the moment a situation falls outside the conventional playbook.

The contract is one input to the credit decision, not the decision itself. Judgment requires holding several considerations all at once and choosing a response that the organization can stand behind later.
Leaders build judgment by exposing team members to how decisions get made, not just to how tasks get done.
They ask team members, “What would you do and why?” and then talk through their own reasoning, including what they gave weight to and what they chose to give up.
The best test of a leader’s influence is not what the team knows. It is how the team decides when the answer is not in the field manual.
Expertise makes people useful. Judgment makes them trustworthy. Good leaders build both.
